quests.instruction: Which shape has 5 sides and 5 corners, right between a square and a hexagon in side count?
quests.hint: This shape has one more side than a square, and one fewer than a hexagon.
quests.explanation: A pentagon's 5 sides sit exactly between a square's 4 and a hexagon's 6.
quests.funFact: Lining up shapes by side count goes: triangle, square, pentagon, hexagon, octagon.

quests.instruction: Which shape has more sides than any other shape you've learned in this game so far?
quests.hint: Think of the shape used for stop signs, with the highest side count yet.
quests.explanation: With 8 sides, an octagon has more straight sides than any shape learned so far.
quests.funFact: If a shape had even more sides, it would start to look almost round, like a circle.

quests.instruction: Which shape has 4 equal sides but a different corner arrangement than a typical square?
quests.hint: Look for the shape whose top and bottom corners point instead of lying flat.
quests.explanation: A diamond has 4 equal sides just like a square, but arranged so its corners point instead of lying flat.
quests.funFact: Some card games use the diamond shape as one of their four playing card suits.

quests.instruction: Which shape matches the cross-section of a new, unsharpened pencil?
quests.hint: Think of a shape with 6 flat sides running the length of the pencil.
quests.explanation: Many pencils have a 6-sided cross-section, just like a hexagon.
quests.funFact: Hexagon pencils are less likely to roll off a slanted desk than round ones.

quests.instruction: Which shape has 4 equal sides and sits flat on one full side, unlike a diamond?
quests.hint: Look for the shape that rests on a flat bottom edge, not a pointed corner.
quests.explanation: A square rests flat on one whole side, while a diamond balances on a single point.
quests.funFact: A square and a diamond can actually be the exact same shape, just turned differently.

quests.instruction: Which shape can be drawn by combining a square with a triangle sitting right on top of it?
quests.hint: Think of a house outline: a square base topped by a pointed roof, drawn as one shape.
quests.explanation: A square topped by a triangle roof combines into one 5-sided pentagon outline.
quests.funFact: Artists often draw simple houses this way because it naturally forms a pentagon.

quests.instruction: Which shape has 8 sides, each one shorter than the sides of a big square drawn the same width?
quests.hint: Think of a square with each corner sliced off to add four extra sides.
quests.explanation: Slicing each corner off a square adds four new sides, turning it into an 8-sided octagon.
quests.funFact: You can turn a square into an octagon just by snipping each corner at an angle.

quests.instruction: Which shape do you get by slicing just two corners off a square, adding two new sides?
quests.hint: A square has 4 sides — slicing two corners adds two more.
quests.explanation: Adding two new sides to a square's 4 sides makes 6 sides total, just like a hexagon.
quests.funFact: Playing with corner cuts is a fun way to see how polygons are related to each other.

quests.instruction: Which shape do you get by slicing just one corner off a square, adding one new side?
quests.hint: A square has 4 sides — slicing one corner adds just one more.
quests.explanation: Adding one new side to a square's 4 sides makes 5 sides total, just like a pentagon.
quests.funFact: This corner-slicing trick shows exactly how a pentagon relates to a square.

quests.instruction: Which shape has no corners to slice off, no matter how you try?
quests.hint: Look for the one shape that never had any corners to begin with.
quests.explanation: A circle never has corners to slice, since its whole edge is one smooth curve.
quests.funFact: This is exactly why circles are considered the roundest and smoothest shape of all.

quests.instruction: Which shape has 3 sides, the fewest of any shape that could be turned into a pentagon by adding sides?
quests.hint: You would need to add 2 sides to this shape to reach a pentagon's 5.
quests.explanation: Adding 2 sides to a triangle's 3 sides makes 5 total, matching a pentagon.
quests.funFact: Triangles are the starting point for building up to almost every other straight-sided shape.

quests.instruction: Which shape needs exactly 5 more sides than a triangle to be complete?
quests.hint: A triangle has 3 sides — this shape needs 5 more to reach its full count.
quests.explanation: Adding 5 sides to a triangle's 3 sides makes 8 total, matching an octagon.
quests.funFact: Counting up from a triangle, you pass through square, pentagon, hexagon, and heptagon before reaching octagon.

quests.instruction: Which shape has a smooth curved edge, but unlike a circle, is clearly longer in one direction?
quests.hint: Look for the shape that curves like a circle but looks a bit stretched.
quests.explanation: An oval curves smoothly like a circle, but stretches longer in one direction.
quests.funFact: Ovals appear anywhere a circle looks gently squeezed or pulled longer.

quests.instruction: Which shape matches the pattern often seen painted on the ground near a garden path?
quests.hint: Think of a shape with 6 sides, like the pattern on a honeycomb.
quests.explanation: Honeycomb-style hexagon patterns are a popular design for garden paths and tiles.
quests.funFact: Hexagon tiles fit together with no wasted space, just like real honeycomb.

quests.instruction: Which shape has 5 sides, the same number of points as a classic star shape?
quests.hint: Count the points on a star — this shape has the same number of sides.
quests.explanation: A pentagon has 5 sides, matching the 5 points of a classic star.
quests.funFact: If you connect the 5 outer points of a star with straight lines, you can draw a pentagon inside it.

quests.instruction: Which shape, if you added just 1 side, would become a pentagon?
quests.hint: Think of the 4-sided shape that is just one side short of a pentagon.
quests.explanation: Adding just 1 side to a square's 4 sides makes 5, turning it into a pentagon.
quests.funFact: This is a handy way to remember that a pentagon has one more side than a square.

quests.instruction: Which shape, if you removed 2 sides, would become a hexagon?
quests.hint: Think of the 8-sided shape that has exactly 2 more sides than a hexagon.
quests.explanation: Removing 2 sides from an octagon's 8 sides leaves 6, turning it into a hexagon.
quests.funFact: This kind of side-counting helps you see how all the polygons connect to each other.

quests.instruction: Which shape, even though it has 4 equal sides like a square, is never described as sitting flat on an edge?
quests.hint: Look for the shape that always seems to be balancing on a corner instead.
quests.explanation: A diamond always appears balancing on a corner, unlike a square which sits flat on an edge.
quests.funFact: This is really just a square, drawn turned on its point instead of its side.

quests.instruction: Which shape appears both in honeycomb cells and on the flat faces of some pencils?
quests.hint: Think of the 6-sided shape shared by bees and pencil makers.
quests.explanation: Both honeycomb cells and many pencils use the 6-sided hexagon shape.
quests.funFact: Hexagons show up in nature and in everyday objects because they fit together so efficiently.

quests.instruction: Which shape appears on both stop signs and some gazebo buildings?
quests.hint: Think of the 8-sided shape shared by road signs and garden buildings.
quests.explanation: Both stop signs and some gazebos use the 8-sided octagon shape.
quests.funFact: An octagon's many flat sides make it useful for both signs and small buildings.

quests.instruction: Which shape appears on both home plate and some simple house drawings?
quests.hint: Think of the 5-sided shape shared by a baseball field and a house outline.
quests.explanation: Both home plate and simple house drawings use the 5-sided pentagon shape.
quests.funFact: Noticing the same shape in different places is a great way to remember it.

quests.instruction: Which shape has points instead of plain corners, setting it apart from a hexagon or pentagon?
quests.hint: Look for the shape with sharp spikes poking outward, not a smooth polygon edge.
quests.explanation: A star has sharp points poking outward, unlike the plain corners of a hexagon or pentagon.
quests.funFact: A star shape is actually made from two overlapping triangles in some classic designs.

quests.instruction: Which shape has 4 sides and 4 corners, but would need 4 MORE sides to become an octagon?
quests.hint: An octagon has 8 sides — this shape has exactly half that many.
quests.explanation: A rectangle's 4 sides are exactly half of an octagon's 8 sides.
quests.funFact: Doubling the sides of a 4-sided shape is one way to imagine building an octagon.

quests.instruction: Which shape has no sides to count at all, making every side-counting question about it a trick question?
quests.hint: Look for the shape that is one continuous curve with nothing to count.
quests.explanation: A circle has no straight sides at all, so there is nothing to count — its edge is one smooth curve.
quests.funFact: Mathematicians describe a circle's edge with a special curved measurement instead of counting sides.

quests.instruction: Which shape sits between a square and a hexagon if you line up shapes by their number of sides?
quests.hint: This shape has one more side than 4, and one fewer than 6.
quests.explanation: A pentagon's 5 sides place it right between a square's 4 and a hexagon's 6.
quests.funFact: Lining shapes up by side count is a great way to see how they're all connected.

quests.instruction: Which shape sits between a pentagon and an octagon if you count up by sides, two at a time?
quests.hint: This shape has one more side than a pentagon, and two fewer than an octagon.
quests.explanation: A hexagon's 6 sides sit between a pentagon's 5 and an octagon's 8.
quests.funFact: Between hexagon and octagon there's actually one more shape you haven't met yet, called a heptagon, with 7 sides.

quests.instruction: Which shape has the most sides of every shape you have learned in this game so far?
quests.hint: Think of the shape used for stop signs — it has more sides than any other shape here.
quests.explanation: With 8 sides, an octagon has more sides than any other shape introduced so far in this game.
quests.funFact: As shapes gain more and more sides, they start to look rounder, closer to a circle.

quests.instruction: Which shape, alongside squares and hexagons, is one of only three regular shapes that tile a floor with zero gaps?
quests.hint: This shape has just 3 sides, the fewest of the three floor-tiling shapes.
quests.explanation: Triangles, squares, and hexagons are the only three regular shapes that tile a floor perfectly, with zero gaps.
quests.funFact: Even though pentagons and octagons are nice shapes, they cannot tile a floor alone without gaps.

quests.instruction: Which shape, like a circle, has zero corners, but is not perfectly round?
quests.hint: Look for the shape that curves smoothly but looks a little stretched compared to a circle.
quests.explanation: An oval has zero corners just like a circle, but it is stretched instead of perfectly round.
quests.funFact: You could think of an oval as a circle's stretched-out cousin.

quests.instruction: Which shape do you get if you keep slicing corners off a hexagon until it has 8 sides?
quests.hint: A hexagon has 6 sides — slicing corners can add just enough to reach 8.
quests.explanation: Slicing corners off a hexagon to add 2 more sides gives you an 8-sided octagon.
quests.funFact: This corner-slicing pattern is a fun way to build up from triangle all the way to octagon.
